title: Explainable Automated Essay Scoring: Deep Learning Really Has Pedagogical Value
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automated essay scoring (AES) as a largely opaque “black box,” especially at the rubric level where teachers and students would need interpretable information to trust and use AI-generated scores and feedback. The authors argue that prior AES work has focused mostly on holistic scoring and has rarely explained how specific writing features lead to rubric scores. They therefore investigate whether explainable AI methods can make AES more transparent, help debug predictive models, and support the future generation of formative feedback during writing.

The study builds on a previously developed AES system using a feature-based deep learning approach. Specifically, the authors train multi-layer perceptron neural networks to predict rubric scores, focusing in this paper on the “style” rubric. Essays are represented using 1,592 linguistic indices derived from natural language processing tools, then reduced through feature selection. The paper evaluates both predictive accuracy and descriptive accuracy of explanations using SHAP, comparing several SHAP implementations (KernelSHAP, DeepSHAP, and GradientSHAP) and testing whether deeper neural networks yield more trustworthy explanations.

The population consists of Grade 7 students’ narrative essays from the ASAP dataset. These essays were written in the context of state-wide assessments in the United States, with an average length of 171 words. Each essay was scored by two human raters on four rubrics: ideas, organization, style, and conventions. The study is not an intervention trial with students; rather, it is a secondary analysis of an existing educational assessment dataset to examine how well explainable AES models perform and how their explanations might be used to inspect or eventually support feedback.

The main conclusions are that deep learning can improve the trustworthiness of explanation models, with descriptive accuracy increasing by about 10% as more hidden layers were added. The study also finds that faster SHAP implementations for deep learning are as accurate as the slower model-agnostic approach, making real-time explanation more feasible. Overall, the paper concludes that explainable deep-learning-based AES has pedagogical value because it can expose important writing features globally and locally, support model debugging, and lay the groundwork for personalized formative feedback, although the pedagogical impact of such feedback on student writing was not evaluated in this study.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An automated essay scoring (AES) system using deep learning and explainable AI to predict rubric-level writing scores and generate interpretable feedback from linguistic features.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an explainable AES system for Grade-7 essays, focusing on the Style rubric. It uses a multi-layer perceptron with SHAP explanations over 1592 linguistic indices (reduced to 282) to score essays and support formative feedback.

findings.finding_summary: On the ASAP Grade-7 essay dataset, the Style rubric scoring model achieved QWK=0.650, exact agreement=54.3%, adjacent-1 agreement=92.5%, and adjacent-2 agreement=99.8% on the testing set. Human raters’ agreement on the Style rubric was QWK=0.54, with 65.3% exact matches and 34.4% adjacent matches, though on a different 0–3 human rating scale versus the model’s resolved 0–6 scale.
findings.measure: Style rubric scoring accuracy on ASAP Grade-7 essays using quadratic weighted kappa and exact/adjacent agreement rates
findings.sample_size: n=1567 essays total; testing set n=314

findings.finding_summary: Faster SHAP implementations for deep learning were reported to be as accurate as the slower model-agnostic KernelSHAP implementation, while improving processing time by up to three orders of magnitude. Independent t-tests found no statistically significant differences between Kernel, Deep, and Gradient explainers on precision, recall, or F1 for descriptive accuracy in the 2-layer ensemble model (all reported p-values > 0.05).
findings.measure: Descriptive accuracy equivalence and processing speed of SHAP implementations
findings.effect_size: up to three orders of magnitude faster; non-significant differences across explainers
findings.sample_size: testing set n=314 essays; 500 iterations per essay for explanation evaluation

findings.finding_summary: As more hidden layers were added to the neural network, descriptive accuracy increased by about 10%, indicating more trustworthy explanations for deeper models. For GradientSHAP explainers, 2-layer vs 6-layer differences were statistically significant for precision, recall, and F1 at both thresholds tested (e.g., p=0.0003 and 0.0001 for precision; p=0.0000 for recall and F1).
findings.measure: Trustworthiness/descriptive accuracy of explanation models across neural network depth
findings.sample_size: testing set n=314 essays; 500 iterations per essay for explanation evaluation

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study evaluating an explainable automated essay scoring system on an existing dataset, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes. The paper mainly assesses model performance, interpretability, and feasibility rather than causal educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive technical performance and interpretability gains, but does not evaluate actual effects on student writing performance or classroom outcomes. Impact on learning is therefore promising but unclear.
